passage: “Hemant, you're my best friend, so you get the whole story. I'm Dilnaz, and my third mock dropped by thirty marks. My first reaction was to panic and blame the paper. Then I made myself look. My sleep log said five hours a night all week. My mistakes were mostly in electrostatics. So I changed two things. I dropped Sunday cricket for two weeks, and I added twenty short physics problems every evening. I'm also writing my mock score, sleep hours and mood on one page each Saturday. Honestly, I don't know yet if it's working. I'll compare the next two mocks and decide from that, not from how I feel.”

passage:
I'm Sangeeta, and I sit behind Nandini in the Saturday mock hall. Her first two mocks were 142 and 150. The third one, she came out looking pale. 118.

That Monday she didn't hide it. She sat on the library steps with her mock sheets and a notebook, and I watched her write two headings: "Sleep" and "Topics". She asked me, "Did you sleep before the third mock?" I said yes. She said she hadn't, much, that week: late nights at her cousin's engagement.

Then she circled physics. Most of the lost marks were in current electricity.

The next week, I noticed she'd stopped going to Sunday badminton. She told me it was only for two weeks. Every day at lunch she did a short set of physics problems, ten or so, with a timer.

Her fourth mock was 139. Fifth, 147. I don't know what she felt, but she looked relieved.

qa.q: What did Nandini score in the third mock?
What might Nandini have been feeling when she came out of the third mock?
qa.a: She probably felt shaken and disappointed, looking pale after the drop.

qa.q: What else could Nandini check if scores drop again?
qa.a: She could look at her sleep and topic gaps again, as she did, and ask a teacher for help if the same topic keeps costing marks.

qa.q: How did Nandini's response look to Sangeeta?
qa.a: To Sangeeta it looked practical and calm: a notebook, a short break from badminton and daily problem sets, though Sangeeta can't know exactly what Nandini felt.

grounding: An observer describes a student who, after a drop in a mock, checks sleep and topic gaps, cuts a weekend activity for two weeks and adds daily physics problem sets.

passage:
Day 1, Sunday evening: Tarun's third mock score was 96, down from 128. He sat with his uncle Ramesh in the courtyard and pulled out a notebook. "First, sleep," he said. "I slept around one all week. Before, it was eleven." Then topics. Physics had dropped the most, mostly mechanics.

Day 3, Tuesday: He told his cricket team he'd skip Saturday matches for two weeks. At lunch he started a small daily set: eight mechanics problems, thirty minutes. He wrote each score on a chart inside his cupboard door. Bed by eleven again.

Day 15, the next Sunday but one: Fourth mock: 118. Physics up by fourteen marks. Tarun showed Ramesh the chart. "Not back to 128 yet. But climbing." Ramesh nodded. "Then you keep the problem sets, and bring cricket back next week?"

"Deal," Tarun said.

qa.q: What was Tarun's third mock score?
How might Tarun have felt when showing Ramesh the chart?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and encouraged, seeing his score climbing again even if not fully back.

qa.q: What else could Tarun track as he brings cricket back?
qa.a: He could keep watching his mock scores and sleep, to make sure adding cricket back does not undo the recovery.

qa.q: How does Tarun's plan look to Ramesh?
qa.a: Ramesh seems supportive and practical, agreeing the problem sets should stay while cricket returns.

grounding: Shows a student who, after a drop in a mock, checks sleep and topic gaps, pauses a weekend activity, adds daily physics problems and tracks whether scores recover.
